newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO chief sees TV ads as weapon in RSI campaign.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO chief sees TV ads as weapon in RSI campaign.

text.p: AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said Monday the 78-union federation would not hesitate to use its television advertising weapon in its campaign to combat repetitive strain injuries (RSI) in the workplace.

Launching a "Stop the Pain" campaign on the day the labour movement marks as "Workers' Memorial Day," Sweeney warned lawmakers that "we will hold them responsible for any further delays" in developing federal ergonomic standards aimed at preventing such injuries.
"We're hoping that we're going to be able to move the debate out of Washington and into the work site," Sweeney told a news conference.

The AFL-CIO used TV ads during last year's election campaign in targeted congressional districts, nearly all of them held by Republicans, to highlight lawmakers' positions on issues such as raising the minimum wage and cutting Medicare coverage.

This year the labour federation has already launched a targeted ad campaign favouring federal money for school repairs and opposing tax breaks for multi-national corporations. Sweeney said lawmakers who oppose the Labour Department's effort to come up with ergonomic standards may be hit with an ad campaign too.

The department's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has been gathering information since the end of last year to propose RSI-safety standards that employers would be required to follow.
Until Sept. 30, 1996 OSHA was barred for nearly two years by the Republican-controlled Congress from spending any money on an ergonomics standard, leaving a draft proposal sidetracked.

RSI, a painful and potentially debilitating injury, is caused by repetitive motion, usually of the hands or arms. It is the fastest growing and costliest of workplace injuries, accounting for one-third of the $60 billion in annual workers' compensation costs.

Sweeney, who said RSI concerns ranked very high in focus groups and mail received by the AFL-CIO, said the "Stop the Pain" campaign also would make greater use of RSI as a union organising issue as well as educating workers about RSI and encouraging them to file complaints with OSHA.

Sweeney also railed against employer groups that have opposed a federal ergonomics standard, some of which criticised the sidetracked OSHA study as a 'one-size-fits-all" solution to a complex problem.

Monday was the American labour movement's ninth annual Workers Memorial Day, a day set aside to highlight workplace hazards and to honour workers who have been killed, injured or made ill while on their jobs.
